newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania C.bank hopeful on new IMF accord.
newsitem.headline: Romania C.bank hopeful on new IMF accord.

text.p: The central bank governor was quoted as saying on Tuesday that Romania hoped for a resumption of IMF credits and economists said the country's image abroad would improve with reformists in charge after elections.

Bank governor Mugur Isarescu told the Romania Libera newspaper that relations with the International Montetary Fund had not been frozen despite the suspension of payments of part of the loan in tranches this year over policy differences.
Romania, he said, had every reason to hope for restoration of a $280 million loan accord and agreement on further credits.
"The National Bank (BNR) maintains a professional and reliable dialogue with the IMF and a new accord could be concluded soon on this basis," Isarescu told the daily.
Romania signed the current IMF accord last December, but the Fund suspended payments this year after expressing concern over restrictions on the local foreign exchange market.
Romanian economists suggested then that the IMF was also displeased at the pace of reforms, including privatisation and restructuring in the ex-communist country.
But they say the chances of restoring IMF credits are much improved since reformists took power in presidential and general elections, ousting ex-communists in power since 1989.
"The new government, including Christian Democrats and Social Democrats, is good news for the growth of Romanian economy," economist Teodor Nicolaescu said.

Academic Emil Constantinescu, elected president at the weekend, is committed to faster economic reforms, mixing tight financial discipline with improved benefits to raise some of the lowest living standards in eastern Europe.

The National Peasant Party, the main component of Constantinescu's electoral bloc which won the most seats in parliamentary elections this month, was choosing its nominees for prime minister and other key posts on Tuesday.
Analysts said the new government would have to tackle currency and budget issues to regain IMF confidence.
The leu currency has been propped up artificially for months on interbank markets, where it stands at about 40 percent above street levels of 4,850 to the dollar.
The state budget gap surged to 2.86 trillion lei ($817 million) in nine months and is forecast to climb to 4.27 trillion by end-1996, some 3.5 percent of Romania's estimated gross domestic product.
Restoring the accord with the IMF could consolidate and expand Romania's access to external financing sources, including international lenders, syndicated loans and bonds markets, Isarescu said.

"What is essential for a new accord is a programme of economic, monetary and budgetary policies, plus restructuring," Isarescu told Romania Libera. "It is the economic policy programme that will give credibility to Romania."
The central bank governor told local media immediately after Constaninescu's election that the BNR would support the new government during a "window of opportunity" to press ahead with new policies.
Former Prime Minister Petre Roman, who heads the Social Democrats, junior partners in the coalition, said relaunching talks with Western financial institutions was a top priority.
"The new government has everything on its side," he told a television interviewer. "All it has to do is send clear signals that it is determined to resume the course of reforms." ($1=3500 Lei)
